items.title: Fix fp32 non-associative gradient summation test threshold
items.body:
## Description
Updated float32 tolerance for fp32 non-associative summation precision limits on hardware whose matmul accumulates below full float32 width. This enables the two `stage_backward_weight` tests pass without weakening precision checks anywhere else.


## Related Issue
PR for related backend (Neuron) usage: https://github.com/aws-neuron/private-torch-neuronx/pull/1523

## Motivation and Context
The default float32 precision for `assert_close` (rtol=1.3e-6,
atol=1e-5) assumes both sides of the comparison reduce in the same order and
accumulate in full-width float32. The `stage_backward_weight` tests compare
split backward (`stage_backward_input` + `stage_backward_weight`) against a
monolithic `.backward()`, i.e. a different reduction order. On CPU/CUDA
that is hidden by full-float32 matmul accumulation; on hardware with
lower-precision matmul accumulation, this assert_close fails and the gradients diverge at
~1e-5. The results are still correct to float32 hardware epsilon.

items.title: feat: grow append in place where the alias analysis proves it safe (#578 steps 3+4)
items.body:
Completes #578. The sieve — the last loss in `bench/native-speed` — now **ties Rust**.

## What changed

At a `v = append(v, x)` site where `machin alias` (#600) proved v has no other live reference across that append, the block is handed to `realloc` instead of copied into a fresh one and abandoned. **Every other append is untouched.**

Two runtime guards the static proof can't express:

1. **Head only** — the arena is singly-linked, so only its most recent allocation grows in place; anything else falls back. Barely a restriction: a tight append loop allocates nothing in between, which is exactly when it matters.
2. **Strlen-cache invalidation** — `mfl_strlen_cached` keys on pointer identity, sound only while the arena frees nothing mid-life. `realloc` hands an address back to the allocator, so the cache is dropped on this path. Missing it would have been a silent wrong-length bug in `substr()`, far from anything resembling `append`.

## Measured on the CI runner, not this laptop

| | machin | Rust | Zig | machin/Rust |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| before | 96.7 ms | 87.7 ms | 73.0 ms | **1.10×** |
| after | 101.9 ms | 100.6 ms | 86.0 ms | **1.01×** |

Absolute ms went *up* because the whole runner was ~15% slower that session — which is precisely why the ratio to a control is what's quoted. The laptop showed a bigger swing (1.46× → 1.06×) because slower memory makes the append penalty a larger share, but it was at 58–68% noise and isn't a publishable source.

**It does not tie Zig** — still ~1.19× behind (from 1.32×). Reported as a remaining gap rather than rounded away.

## Verification

- **ASan adversarial suite (#601) stays green** — every live-alias-across-append shape still reads correct data.
- **Emission checked both ways**: the sieve gets 1 owned call site; a program that aliases before appending gets 0.
- **Differential output**: 49 of 49 deterministic examples byte-identical. The 50th, `goroutines.mfl`, differs — but it's nondeterministic by nature (the *old* compiler gives three different outputs in three runs) and contains zero appends.
- Full suite green — `ok machin 249.496s`.

## Docs

Corrects the standing explanation everywhere: the sieve gap was **never slice indexing** — that loop always tied Rust. The README's kernel table is explicitly marked as predating the fix rather than left looking current.

items.title: fix(memory): close three gaps found by the eval suite
items.body:
## Summary
The first subscription-billed eval baseline (docs/superpowers/reports/2026-08-02-ghost-eval.md) surfaced several real problems. This closes three of them:

- **`docs/superpowers/eval/lib/seed-project.sh`** filtered the real DB by `WHERE id = '<project-name>'`, but `ghost reflect <name>` resolves projects by `name`, not `id`. Real projects registered by absolute path have a hashed `id` different from their `name` (e.g. `id=6bdc098af7f5, name=ghost`), so seeding silently copied zero rows for `ghost`/`infra` and every downstream `ghost reflect`/`resolve`/`supersede` call correctly reported "project not found" against a genuinely-empty scratch DB. `roller` only worked because its `id` happens to equal its `name`. Fixed to resolve the real `id` by name-or-id first, filter everything on that, and fail loudly (instead of silently seeding zero rows) if nothing or no memories match.
- **Save-time dedup (`Store.Upsert`)** missed near-duplicate restatements of the same fact at different lengths — Jaccard punishes the wordier side's extra filler tokens, so paraphrases scored 0.2–0.45, under the 0.5 merge threshold. Added a gated overlap-coefficient leg (min 5 tokens, min 0.6 length ratio on the shorter/longer side) that catches genuine restatements without merging a short save that's merely a subset of an unrelated longer memory.
- **Supersession never propagated to ranking.** `SupersedeDemote` existed in `vector.go` but defaulted `false` with no caller ever setting it, so a reversed memory could still outrank its replacement in `ghost_memory_search` — flipped on by default (hard no-op without an explicit `ghost supersede --apply`-created edge). Decisions never got a writer for their existing `status`/`superseded_by` columns either; added `Store.SupersedeDecision` and an optional `supersedes` arg on `ghost_decision_record`, and `ListDecisions` now truncates to the newest N first, then sorts superseded rows last within that window (so demotion can't push a reversal out of the results).

The eval's other two `resolve`/`supersede` "project not found" failures were investigated and are **not Ghost bugs** — the storyline scenario gave the actor session an empty scratch cwd with no codebase, so it correctly refused to fabricate a root cause and never called any Ghost write tool, and the harness never fails when a storyline turns out to be a scenario-writing gap rather than a Ghost issue. No code change needed there.

## Test plan
- [x] `go vet ./...` — clean
- [x] `go test ./...` — all packages pass except `internal/supersede`'s `TestHaikuClassifierLive`, which requires real Anthropic API credits (`anthropic credit balance too low`) and fails identically on `main` — pre-existing, unrelated to this change.
- [x] `seed-project.sh` manually verified against throwaway DBs: seed-by-name (id != name), seed-by-raw-id, legacy id==name, unknown project (exit 1), empty project (exit 1), SQL-injection string rejected pre-query.
- [x] New unit tests: `TestStoreUpsertMergesLengthAsymmetricParaphrases`, `TestSupersedeDemoteClearsFrontier`, `TestListDecisionsLimitPicksNewestNotLiveOnly`, `TestDecisionRecordSupersedesArg`, plus existing decision/vector suites.

End-of-day wrapup. Two files.

## `CHANGELOG.md`

The v5.8.0 section documented the four correctness fixes — those were added during release prep in #343 — but **none of the benchmarking, CI or documentation work that shipped in the same release**. None of #319, #320, #321, #322, #327, #329, #330 or #333 appeared anywhere in the file.

| section | added |
|---|---|
| **Added** | the benchmark results site; the benchmark-build CI lane; the Highway SIMD lane |
| **Changed** | #82 gate asserts the median with a per-size floor; `SPARSE_SIZES` default lowered to a size that completes; CI runs on draft → ready; `cmake --preset release` builds something |
| **Fixed** | `bench_klu` / `bench_superlu` did not compile; `bench_sparse`'s 3-D Laplacian grid is clamped |

These are documentation of what v5.8.0 already contains — the tag is unchanged, and the auto-generated release notes already reflected the commits.

## `docs/sessions/2026-08-02-*.md`

Follows the existing session-doc format (Objective / Context / Work Completed / Decisions & Rationale / Outcome / Issues & PRs).

The connecting thread it records: **every defect found this session lived in code that a test or lane appeared to cover but structurally could not** — n=2 and n=3 for Bunch–Kaufman where no interchange is possible, small structured matrices for SVD, plain arithmetic accumulators for the norms, "does the solve converge" for `ilu_0`, and for the tooling bugs, source files no runner compiled at all.

Three decisions worth carrying forward:

- **Fix the cause, not the instance.** Three of the four bugs shipped with a correct one-line fix in the issue, and in each the real problem was redundant or ambiguous state. `ilu_0` stored the diagonal twice with one of two consumers filtering it; storing it once makes the invariant structural. `two_norm<Acc>` could have rounded to `mag_t` and compiled, but that discards what the accumulator bought.
- **Tests must assert the failing regime is live** — that an interchange occurred, that a 2×2 block appeared, that ILU(0) was exact — otherwise they can quietly stop covering the bug, which is exactly how these survived.
- **Publish the negative results.** `ilu_0` is unchanged at 29 BiCGSTAB iterations on a 2-D Laplacian; only the tridiagonal case goes 11 → 1. And the retracted N=465 gate claim stays visible on the results page rather than being silently rewritten.

Session docs are not registered in `FILE_MAP`, matching the existing ones — they stay GitHub-only.

`npm run build` — 43 pages, unchanged. Changelog structure intact (one `### Changed` in the 5.8.0 section, no duplicated headings).

## New Features
- Implemented core database engine with Query Optimizer and Bulk Storage capabilities.
- Added modular storage architecture featuring Bulk and Memory bridges for caching and JSONL collection monitoring.
- Integrated automated backup query recovery system and `db.logsys` features.
- Added multi-tab query editor with Monaco integration and authentication management.
- Implemented REST API endpoints for database management and AI query assistance.
- Added UUID v7 support and migrated default `_id` generation.
- Added support for database clock time zone configuration through settings.
- Resolved key duplication in `sysvaults` type collections.
- Implemented collection definitions and hybrid memory-disk caching, indexing, and thread-safe data operations.
- Added `CaseInsensitiveDocumentWrapper` for case-insensitive data access.

## Fixes & Refactoring
- Refactored `resultset` functions and added a default serializable `toList()` conversion for `select` functions used in JOINs.

items.title: feat: targeted supersede demote — the staleness fix that clears the recency-trap frontier
items.body:
The payoff of the recency-trap experiment (#184). That experiment proved a *global* recency prior can't fix staleness by default — it's a cliff, every weight that helps staleness destroys old-but-correct retrieval. This is the *targeted* fix that clears the frontier, shipped off by default.

## Mechanism

`SearchParams.SupersedeDemote` (default false) + `Store.SupersedesWithin`: within the returned result window, demote a memory below every present memory that supersedes it, using directed `supersedes` links. Penalty = count of present superseders, stable-sorted — so update chains (v3→v2→v1, star links) order correctly, and it's a **hard no-op** when no `supersedes` edge joins two results. Applied on all three `SearchHybridParams` return paths, after recency.

No schema change: `supersedes` and `source='llm'` were already in the `memory_links` CHECK.

## The headline (`TestSupersedeDemoteClearsFrontier`)

| | staleness fresh-wins | recency-trap correct-wins |
|---|---|---|
| default (off) | 0.083 | 0.929 |
| **supersede demote on** | **1.000** | **0.929** (untouched) |

It flips staleness to 100% **while leaving the recency-trap exactly where it was** — the free lunch a global recency weight provably could not be. The trap is untouched because its distractors aren't supersession pairs (no `supersedes` edge exists between them), so the demote never fires on them. This is the whole argument for doing the targeted work instead of the cheap global one, now demonstrated.

## Scope: consumption now, creation next

This PR is the **consumer**, proven against seeded ground-truth links, and inert in production (off by default; graded benchmarks have no supersedes links, so `ghost bench` hybrid NDCG@10 stays 0.989 and ranking is byte-identical). The **creator** — an LLM classifier emitting star `supersedes` links at reflection time — is the next roadmap item and the harder half: it must contend with reflection's cascade-delete of links (`ReplaceNonManual` reinserts memories with new IDs), and the cosine linking worker is rejected as creator (symmetric similarity can't assign direction — the same failure that got the graph bonus disabled). I'll bring that as a plan.

`go test -race ./...` green; vet clean; diff-scoped lint 0 issues; docs/benchmarks.md Phase 3 + README updated.

tests to be skipped on 2-device hosts that can run them fine. Lowered the
gate to `@skip_if_lt_x_gpu(2)` to match the actual world size the tests use.

items.title: docs(plan): record the resolved speed picture
items.body:
Completes the plan's Part 2 with what today actually established. The earlier update captured the first measurement; four corrections followed, and the corrections are the useful part.

## The benchmarks were lying in two different ways

Fixed and shipped in #7403. Discarding the result let Perry eliminate the loop; and even with it consumed, `fibonacci(FIB_N)` is loop-invariant, so it hoists out and runs **once** — checksum correct, `TOTAL` zero.

| benchmark | was reported | actually |
|---|---|---|
| `bench_fibonacci` | ~240× faster | **2.5× faster** |
| `bench_bitwise` | ∞ faster | **20.4× SLOWER** |

## The fast path already exists

`bench_bitwise`'s hot loop has **no runtime helper calls at all** — 4 `frem` per iteration, `4 × bl _fmod`, 1754 profile samples. But `expr/binary.rs:588` already emits guarded `srem` with the IEEE `-0` correction. The gap is the analysis, reduced to one line (#7404):

```ts
let a = 12345678; … a % 1000            // srem — fires
let a = 12345678; … a % 1000; a = a + 1 // frem — lost
```

Four wrong hypotheses about that subsystem are recorded so they aren't retried, along with why a careless widening is dangerous: it returns silently wrong integer arithmetic that `===` tests cannot see.

## A measured negative result

`js_array_grow`'s HOLE-init loop is **already vectorised** (6 `stp` in the baseline), so the `slice::fill` rewrite proposed for #7396 measures nothing. The contrary reading came from grepping a symbol absent from a stripped binary — `grep -c` returns 0 whether or not the pattern exists.

## Method notes strengthened

Third instance today of a check that could not fail, and a new one worth its own line: **a fix that compiles, passes every correctness test, and changes no emitted instruction is a fix to the wrong site.** The guarded `srem` I wrote for #7404 passed the entire `-0` edge-case table and emitted zero `srem`.

items.title: Collapse prepared axis batch passes
items.body:
## What changed

- encode independent prepared WGPU axis reductions in one compute pass per batch instead of one pass per reduction
- strengthen the batch contract with mixed sum/min value-semantic coverage
- extend the comparative harness with an eight-reduction prepared batch whose outputs are checked against Leto
- record the matched local A/B samples and measurement limitations

## Why

The prepared batch already used one command buffer, but opening eight compute passes retained avoidable host-side pass construction overhead. Independent reductions can switch pipelines and bind groups inside one pass without new storage or changes to reduction arithmetic.

## Evidence

- `cargo nextest run -p hephaestus-wgpu axis_reductions_match_leto_reference --offline`: 1 passed
- warning-denied Clippy for `hephaestus-wgpu` all targets with `cuda-comparative`: passed on nightly GNU

- local MSVC verification is independently blocked in `backtrace 0.3.76` by missing COFF/Gimli optional dependencies; hosted CI is the authoritative clean-environment gate

The generated `Cargo.lock` update active in the shared main tree is intentionally excluded from this branch.

## High-level PR Summary
This PR optimizes the prepared axis-reduction batch encoding in the WGPU backend by collapsing eight separate compute passes into a single compute pass per batch. items.title: Denovo module updates
items.body:
## Summary

This PR addresses feedback from two external reviewers on the *de novo*
sequencing (DDA-HCD) module, received during community review. Each
reviewer's comment is quoted or paraphrased below, followed by how it was
addressed — including cases where a deliberate decision was made *not*
to change something, for transparency.

---

## Reviewer 1

### 1. Average precision (AUC)
**Comment:** Reporting average precision (area under the precision-coverage
curve) is more informative than precision at 100% coverage alone.

- [x] Added AUC as a metric option. Removed the "recall" toggle (see 3.
  below for why) and added a second tab on the in-depth plot showing full
  precision-coverage curves.

### 2. Amino acid substitutions (I/L, Q/E)
**Comment:** Most evaluations allow I/L substitution; uncertain whether
Q/E should also be allowed — worth showing both ways.

- [x] Added a toggle to allow/disallow I/L ambiguity and a separate toggle
  for Q/E (deamidation) ambiguity, so results can be viewed either way.

### 3. Recall is not well-defined for de novo sequencing
**Comment:** The notion of a false negative (required for a standard
recall definition) doesn't apply to de novo sequencing, since there's no
true negative class.

- [x] Removed "recall" from the module. Replaced with **coverage**
  (proportion of spectra for which a prediction was made) and **AUC**
  (area under the precision-coverage curve), which don't rely on an
  undefined false-negative concept.

### 4. Database search vs. matching precision
**Comment:** Worth evaluating precision by matching predicted peptides
(≥8 amino acids) against a reference proteome, as a complement to the
standard database-search gold standard.

- [x] Added this as a new in-depth plot: a stacked bar chart per tool
  showing the proportion of predictions that are **correct**,
  **incorrect but present in the reference proteome ("in FASTA")**, or
  **incorrect and not found in the proteome**.

---

## Reviewer 2

### 1. Main benchmarking plot is hard to interpret
**Comment:** Plotting amino-acid-level and peptide-level metrics against
each other may obscure interpretation, since different tools show
different AA-vs-peptide performance profiles with different
implications. Suggested separate swarmplots, or at minimum fixing the
axis ranges to [0, 1].

- [x] Kept the combined scatterplot (rather than switching to
  swarmplots), but fixed both axis ranges to [0, 1] and added
  quadrant-based color coding with explicit labels describing what a
  tool's position in each corner implies. Applied the same treatment to
  the PTM-related scatterplots.

### 2. Recall vs. coverage
**Comment:** Coverage is a clearer concept than recall for de novo
sequencing tools (see linked reference).

- [x] Same fix as Reviewer 1, item 3 above — recall replaced with
  coverage and AUC.

### 3. I/L should not be treated as equivalent in exact matching
**Comment:** Isoleucine and leucine should not automatically be
considered equivalent in exact-match evaluation, given evidence some
tools can distinguish them.

- [x] Addressed via the same I/L toggle described in Reviewer 1, item 2 —
  equivalence is now optional rather than assumed.

### 4. Terminology inconsistency (tooltip vs. docs)
**Comment:** The plot menu says "Mass-based" while the tooltip says
"Match-based"; mass tolerance units are described inconsistently
(Da vs. ppm) across different doc sections.

- [x] Fixed. Terminology and units are now consistent between the UI,
  tooltips, and documentation.

### 5. Benchmark Results table columns
**Comment:** Current columns seem tool-specific and may not be relevant
for all submissions; worth clarifying which are expected to be
standardized vs. tool-dependent.

- [ ] **Not changed in this PR.** Columns are kept as-is for now. Open to
  revisiting in a follow-up once we've gathered feedback from more tool
  submissions on which columns are actually useful across the board.

---

# Closing remark

Finally, I'd like to thank both reviewers for their contributions! Feel free to comment further and we'll gladly accomodate/discuss any points related to the module

items.title: docs: postmortem — why the chain loses to one agent, + 4 corrections [OPERATOR-PR]
items.body:
A four-agent evidence re-read (one on Fable) of the replay run tree, the
same-week single-agent control, and the chain source. Adds
`POSTMORTEM-2026-08-11.md`, corrects four things #321 got wrong, and rebuilds
the README's central table around the matched comparison.

## The hypothesis we most wanted tested is REFUTED

The chain does **not** degrade the dev's spec. In the bench arm there is no PM,
SM or contract — the dev's story **is** the raw problem statement, byte-shared
with the control through one template (`swebench_adapter.py:2193`, "one string,
four arms"). The chain loses on what it adds *around* an identical spec.

## Why it loses — five mechanisms, largest first

1. **It slices the dev's horizon.** Every attempt is a fresh sandbox capped at
   **1,800 s** (`runner.py:68`) while the arm clock is 5,400 s. The control's
   **winning** `exstruct-113` run took **1,807 s — longer than any chain attempt
   is allowed to live**. `vyper-4801`'s three attempts each died at the cap with
   `files_touched: []`: 6,341 s and $13.50 for **zero completed dev
   conversations**. The chain is not short of iterations — it buys *more* (2,058
   tool calls vs 1,169). The constraint is **continuity**.
2. **Its gates emit signals the dev cannot decode.** `exstruct-113`'s retry
   prompt contains `Summary: tests not green after run` directly above a tail
   reading `11 passed in 0.82s`, with no reason. Two retries were spent replaying
   an identical disagreement; the other two died to infra. Final diff: 0
   production bytes, $8.83. The control resolved it.
3. **Its verdict layer runs at chance.** P(resolved | green) = 58%,
   P(resolved | blocked) = 50%, base rate 56%.
4. **Its workspace corrupts its own evidence.** On `canvasapi-716` the reviewer
   called the production fix correct, demanded one more test, and the dev's edits
   hit `[Errno 13] Permission denied` on the 0444-locked file — the chain
   demanded, forbade, then punished the absence of the same edit.
5. **The tax is the dev loop re-executing itself**, not the extra personas:
   dev $76.82 of $81.00; 40 fresh conversations for 18 instances, 9 eaten whole
   by infrastructure, 34.6 M fresh input tokens vs the control's 6.4 M.

The identity `score = capability − tax + selection` is incomplete: capability is
not a constant the chain taxes, it is a function of
`(model, task, horizon_slice, policy, environment)`, and shipped work carries a
verdict-recall multiplier.

## Four corrections to #321

- **`line-bot-981` was NOT the dev's gitlink surgery.** That row's trajectories
  contain **no dev git plumbing at all** — only a chain `worktree_create`. It is
  a **workspace-preparation** defect. `tox-3931` *is* dev-side. A prompting fix
  would not have closed the second hole.
- **The arms are not budget-matched, and `swebench_adapter.py:4831` claims they
  are.** Iteration caps match (600); per-conversation wall clock does not
  (1,800 vs 5,400). Undisclosed asymmetry, biased **in the chain's favour**.
- **`exstruct-113` as "not machinery-attributable" is too kind** — it is a
  feedback-channel failure, a category the criterion does not model.
- **The 56% headline omits the operational number.** Three of the ten resolves
  ended in blocked states that would never merge. **Under live-chain semantics
  the factory is 7/18 = 39%.**

## The oracle is unenforced *and* often vacuous

`gate_enforced` is `false` on all 18 rows, yet authoring sits on the critical
path before the dev's first call. **7 of 18 oracle files contain zero asserts** —
the persona mandates HTTP-only tests with no app imports, and 7 of these repos
are libraries with no HTTP surface, so the author correctly emits a pure
`pytest.skip`. This **inverts the obvious fix**: enabling the gate would have
blocked 7 rows, 3 of which resolved — roughly 10/18 → 7/18.

## Verification

Docs-only: **0 Python files touched**. Full suite `-n 4` shows the same 5
acceptance-oracle failures as the `origin/main` baseline measured under identical
conditions — the documented contention class; they pass 70/70 in isolation.
